papers.title_in_file: Experimental data re-uploading with provable enhanced learning capabilities
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections II to VI (model, VC dimension and trainability, apparatus, results, discussion); the Supplementary Material was skimmed only at its start
papers.what_it_is: A photonic single-qubit data re-uploading classifier, with a VC-dimension argument that keeping encoding and processing gates separate gives provable generalization.

assertions.value: The authors report implementing a data re-uploading scheme on a photonic integrated processor that achieves high accuracies in several image classification tasks, and state that it needs only one-qubit states and a sequence of Mach-Zehnder interferometers.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section VI Discussion, p.8
quotes: we present the implementation of a data re-uploading scheme on a photonic integrated processor, achieving high accuracies in several image classification tasks.

Our experimental results show that with a minimum of resources, i.e. one qubit states and a sequence of MZIs, the data re-uploading scheme can be effectively used for binary image classification tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experiment; accuracies are given in Fig. 5, not in the quotes.
assertions.reader_inference: The task set is small (circles, moons, tetromino, overhead MNIST) and binary; the paper makes no advantage claim over classical classifiers.

assertions.value: The paper proves that the original data re-uploading scheme, with encoding and rotation as separate gates, has a finite VC dimension, whereas the compressed scheme has an infinite one, and concludes that the original scheme is proven to generalize to unknown data.
assertions.anchor: Section III and Fig. 4 caption, pp.5-7
quotes: This implies that the compressed scheme has an infinite VC dimension, while ours is finite
Hence, from a theoretical point of view, the original scheme, implemented in our work, is proven to generalize to unknown data.
assertions.certainty_reason: VC-dimension derivation in Section III, pp.6-7, with Supplementary Material note I.
assertions.reader_inference: Finite VC dimension gives a PAC-style generalization guarantee for this single-qubit model only; it says nothing about multi-qubit or practical models.

assertions.value: The authors state that their claims about trainability and generalizability of the compressed scheme rest on worst-case examples and might not be as dramatic in other tasks.
quotes: Despite the promising results, the above statements about trainabilty and generalizabilty for the compressed scheme are worst-case examples and might not be as dramatic in other tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the limit of their comparison, Section VI, p.8.

papers.title_in_file: Benchmarking Metaheuristic-Integrated QAOA against Quantum Annealing
papers.version_note: File is arXiv 2309.16796v3 dated 17 Jan 2024; the record id carries 2024, the file path says 2023.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 2 background (skimmed), Section 3.1 and 3.2 start, Section 4 Results and Discussion, Section 5 Conclusion
papers.what_it_is: A simulator benchmark of QAOA with four metaheuristic optimizers against D-Wave quantum annealing on random number partitioning QUBOs.

assertions.value: The authors report that all four metaheuristic optimizers gave significantly better accuracy than standard QAOA circuits, at significantly worse timing, and that quantum annealing and standard QAOA were by far the fastest.
assertions.anchor: Section 4 Results and Discussion, pp.12-14; Section 5 Conclusion, p.15
quotes: All metaheuristic optimizers performed significantly better in terms of accuracy compared to standard QAOA circuits.

Although quantum speedup benefits were lost, and the metaheuristic circuit timing is significantly worse than standard QAOA and not comparable to Quantum Annealing, the accuracy was dramatically improved using the metaheuristics.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulator study; figures only, no table of numbers in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: Results are on very small instances, so the finding says little about scaling.

assertions.value: The authors state that times and accuracy were averaged over 5 randomly sampled inputs with 4, 8 and 12 input variables, run on the QASM Simulator with default settings, and that the benchmark problem is the Number Partitioning Problem.
quotes: The times and accuracy were computed as an average of 5 randomly sampled inputs across 4, 8, and 12 input variables. All tests were done on the QASM Simulator using default settings.
The paper benchmarks each algorithm's performance in solving the Number Partitioning Problem (NPP)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup, Section 4, p.12.
assertions.reader_inference: Five instances per size and a noise-free simulator limit what the comparison can support.

assertions.value: The authors state that the impact of noise was not investigated and that further testing on noisy quantum machines is future work.
quotes: Future research will investigate the impact of noise.
Further testing will be done on noisy quantum machines to test if performance tapers with quantum noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section 4 p.12 and Section 5 p.15.

papers.title_in_file: Minimal Quantum Reservoirs with Hamiltonian Encoding
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, start of Section II, Section III Results and Discussion, Section IV Conclusions; the middle of Section II (model derivation) was skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of a memoryless quantum reservoir whose input is encoded in Hamiltonian parameters, with delay embeddings added in post-processing for time-series prediction.

assertions.value: The authors report, from numerical simulation, that a minimal quantum reservoir without intrinsic memory can perform nonlinear regression and prediction tasks when augmented with post-processing delay embeddings, and that a reservoir of N = 5 qubits performs the pointwise nonlinear synthesis task with a remarkable degree of accuracy.
quotes: We demonstrate that such a minimal quantum reservoir, despite lacking intrinsic memory, can perform nonlinear regression and prediction tasks when augmented with post-processing delay embeddings.
Fig. 5(c) demonstrates a QR with N = 5 qubits is able to perform the task with a remarkable degree of accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: Result from one numerical simulation study; NMSE values are given in the paper but not quoted here.
assertions.reader_inference: The results are simulations of an idealized dissipative system, not hardware runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study does not directly benchmark quantum against classical reservoirs and involved no analysis of experimental data.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Conclusions, p.10; Data availability, p.11
quotes: While the present study does not directly benchmark quantum against classical reservoirs, it provides a principled baseline for future work exploring quantum advantage.
This research did not involve the analysis of any experimental data.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of scope, Section IV p.10 and Data availability p.11.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantum advantage over a classical reservoir is shown or claimed.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for temporal prediction, the absence of memory imposes a fundamental constraint, and report that the NMSE decreases monotonically as the number of delays increases.
assertions.anchor: Section III, pp.9-10; Section IV, p.10
quotes: For temporal prediction, the absence of memory imposes a fundamental constraint
the NMSE decreasing monotonically as the number of delays increases
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from numerical experiments in Figs. 6 and 7.
assertions.reader_inference: The delay embedding is classical post-processing, so the temporal capacity comes partly from the classical side.

papers.title_in_file: QDCNN: Quantum Deep Learning for Enhancing Safety and Reliability in Autonomous Transportation Systems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Methodology (skimmed), Results text on accuracy and noise, Discussion and Conclusion; tables and figures not available in text
papers.what_it_is: A simulated quantum shadow-detection and lane-direction pipeline for self-driving cars, compared against a classical DNN and classical shadow-detection methods.

assertions.value: The authors report a QDCNN shadow detection time of 0.0049352 seconds, against 0.03 seconds for intensity-based thresholding, 1.47 seconds for chromaticity-based shadow detection and 2.05 seconds for local binary pattern techniques.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section IV Conclusion, p.10
quotes: achieving a shadow detection time of just 0.0049352 seconds, faster than classical algorithms like intensity-based thresholding (0.03 seconds), chromaticity-based shadow detection (1.47 seconds), and local binary pattern techniques (2.05 seconds).
based on photonic quantum gate operation times [34], which ranges from picoseconds to femtoseconds assuming 1000 runs
assertions.certainty_reason: The quantum time is derived from assumed gate operation times, not measured on a device.
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum figure is an estimate from assumed photonic gate times, compared with measured classical run times; it is not a like-for-like timing.

assertions.value: The authors report that on Track 2 the best quantum result was 0.6 accuracy using the VQC, while the classical DNN outperformed the quantum model with 0.70 validation accuracy.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Conclusion, p.10; Section III Results
quotes: and 0.6 on Track 2 using the VQC.
On Track 2, the DNN outperforms the quantum model, achieving 0.70 validation accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's claim of superior accuracy is not supported on this dataset by the paper's own reported numbers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the proposed QDCNN is resource-efficient, using grayscale images and requiring only one qubit and two gates.
quotes: The proposed QDCNN is resource-efficient, using grayscale images and requiring only one qubit and two gates
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the model's size, Section IV p.10.
assertions.reader_inference: A one-qubit model is classically simulable, so a speed claim over classical methods needs the assumed gate times to carry the argument.

papers.title_in_file: A Universal Quantum Algorithm for Weighted Maximum Cut and Ising Problems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 4 Experimental Results, Section 5 Conclusion; the algorithm derivation in Sections 2 and 3 was not read in detail
papers.what_it_is: A shallow-depth hybrid variational circuit for weighted MaxCut and Ising problems, benchmarked in simulation against QAOA and on D-Wave hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that their uqmaxcut approach outperforms the state-of-the-art QAOA by lower depth, by the computed approximation ratios and by a higher probability of outputting optimal solutions.
quotes: The resulting Universal Quantum maxcut (uqmaxcut) approach outperforms the state-of-the-art quantum approximate optimization algorithms (qaoa) by the lower depth, by the computed approximation ratios and by a higher probability of outputting optimal solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study on random graphs.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison used a tuned gradient setup for uqmaxcut; the paper notes QAOA with that optimizer was not competitive, so QAOA was also run with COBYLA.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results are for fully connected graphs of n = 3, 5 and 10 nodes, averaged over 20 graph instances for each n, with the gate-based circuits simulated in a noise-free framework.
quotes: The results are presented in fig. 5 for fully connected graphs of n = 3, 5 and 10 nodes with strictly positive edge weights.
For each n, the results are averaged over 20 graph instances
simulated in a noise-free framework using the QisKit library and the IBM-QASM simulator
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark setup, Section 4, pp.9-10.
assertions.reader_inference: Graphs of at most 10 nodes are far below practical problem sizes.

assertions.value: The authors report that all gate-based methods hardly return a global solution for larger n, and that uqmaxcut returns a global minimizer significantly more often than QAOA and less often than D-Wave.
quotes: All gate-based methods hardly return a global solution for larger n.
returns a global minimizer significantly more often than qaoa and less often than d-wave
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study with D-Wave hardware runs.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion that uqmaxcut can compete with D-Wave holds for the approximation ratio and weaker for the global-solution rate.

papers.title_in_file: Hardware-Aware Quantum Kernel Design Based on Graph Neural Networks
papers.version_note: The file name says Liu-et-al 2025, but the file is arXiv 2506.21161v3 dated 18 Apr 2026 with Fanxu Meng as first author. It is the paper the record names.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, the experimental setup and PST/KTA prediction results text, dataset setup, Conclusion; the method sections were skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A framework that uses graph neural network predictors of circuit fidelity and kernel-target alignment to pick hardware-compatible quantum kernel circuits, evaluated in noisy simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the Credit Card, MNIST-5 and FMNIST-4 benchmark datasets their method consistently outperforms existing baselines in classification accuracy under noisy simulation.
quotes: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including Credit Card (CC), MNIST-5, and FMNIST-4, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing baselines in classification accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study; accuracy values are in figures only.
assertions.reader_inference: Baselines are quantum kernel methods; the abstract does not state a comparison against classical kernels.

assertions.value: The authors state that simulations used system sizes of N = 4, 5, 7, and 8 qubits, that these scales are relatively small, and that they are sufficient to demonstrate the approach under NISQ-relevant conditions.
quotes: we conduct simulations across different system sizes with N = 4, 5, 7, and 8 qubits. Although these scales are relatively small, they are sufficient to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach under NISQ-relevant conditions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its simulation scale, Section 4, p.12.
assertions.reader_inference: Whether the result holds at larger sizes is untested here.

assertions.value: The authors state that extending the framework to larger-scale quantum systems beyond the reach of classical simulation remains an important direction.
quotes: extending the framework to larger-scale quantum systems beyond the reach of classical simulation remains an important direction.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section 5, p.17.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the Credit Card task, 1,000 samples are drawn while ensuring that at least 5% correspond to fraudulent transactions.
quotes: For the CC task, 1,000 samples are drawn while ensuring that at least 5% correspond to fraudulent transactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its dataset setup, Section 4, p.17.
assertions.reader_inference: A 1,000-sample subset is a small base for any fraud-detection conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: Realizing Quantum Kernel Models at Scale with Matrix Product State Simulation
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, start of Section II, Section III Results (A and B), Section IV Conclusion; Section II method details were skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A matrix product state simulation framework for quantum kernels, used with an SVM on the Elliptic Bitcoin data set at up to 165 features and 6400 training points, with CPU and GPU runtime comparison (first author at HSBC, others at Quantinuum).

assertions.value: The authors report a quantum kernel classification task on the Elliptic Bitcoin data set with 165 features and 6400 training data points, run with a Matrix Product State simulator, and state that quantum kernel model performance improves as the feature dimension and training data increase.
quotes: We develop a quantum kernel framework using a Matrix Product State (MPS) simulator and employ it to perform a classification task with 165 features and 6400 training data points, well beyond the scale of any prior work.
We model performance with a quantum kernel computed using our simulator, with the SVM model applied to the Elliptic Bitcoin data set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one noiseless simulation study on one data set.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself sees overfitting with 300 samples and reads the gain as needing more training data; the data set is financial transaction data (illicit versus licit).

assertions.value: The authors report that, in experiments using 50 features, their quantum kernel outperformed the baseline Gaussian kernel.
assertions.anchor: Section III-B, p.7; Section IV Conclusion, p.8
quotes: We now report on experiments aimed to elucidate the effect of circuit complexity on model performance using 50 features.
We find our quantum kernel method outperformed the baseline Gaussian kernel
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; Table II values are not in the quotes.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the smallest-coefficient quantum models did not outperform the classical model, and each run used 6 data samples, so the margin is small and configuration-dependent.

assertions.value: The authors report that increasing the circuit depth significantly diminishes model performance on the test data set.
assertions.anchor: Section III-B and Table III, p.8
quotes: Increasing the depth significantly diminishes model performance on the test data set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study (Table III).
assertions.reader_inference: The authors link this to kernel concentration, a cited known effect.

assertions.value: The authors state that their simulations are virtually noiseless.
quotes: We reiterate that our simulations are (virtually) noiseless
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section IV, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: Hardware noise is known to hurt kernels; none of these results address it.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum simulation for strongly interacting fermions with neutral atoms array : towards the simulation of materials of interest
papers.partial_detail: Front matter, Section 5.9 Conclusion of the Hubbard chapter, and Chapter 6 Summary and outlook; the rest of this PhD thesis (about 6,700 lines of text) was not read
papers.what_it_is: A PhD thesis proposing two hybrid algorithms for Rydberg neutral-atom processors: a digital-analog eigensolver for molecules and a slave-spin method for the Fermi-Hubbard model.

assertions.value: The author reports that a hybrid digital-analog algorithm was numerically tested on the H2, LiH and BeH2 molecules, and that the ground-state energy can be estimated for several inter-atomic distances to a few percent points of error.
quotes: This algorithm has been numerically tested on the H2,LiH and BeH2 molecules.
We show that one can estimate the groundstate energy of the molecules for several molecular inter-atomic distances to a few percent points of error
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result from one thesis, summarized in the outlook chapter without the underlying data.
assertions.reader_inference: These are tiny molecules and the thesis summary gives no comparison with classical methods.

assertions.value: The author states that an important next step is experimental validation with larger atom numbers than the 12 atoms simulated in the Fermi-Hubbard work.
quotes: An important step is an experimental validation with larger atom numbers than the 12 atoms we simulated here.
assertions.certainty_reason: The author's own stated limit, Section 5.9, p.87.
assertions.reader_inference: The slave-spin proposal has not been run on hardware.

assertions.value: The author states that both algorithms developed in the thesis could be implemented on a real device today.
quotes: Experimentally, both algorithms developed in this manuscript could be implemented on real device today.
The two proposed hybrid algorithms are implementable on a NISQ computer, the RQP, and therefore can be run on real device really soon.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's forward-looking claim with no hardware run in the thesis.
assertions.reader_inference: The same chapter says it is far from a forgone conclusion that quantum computing will replace classical electronic-structure methods.
